## TL;DR

This task exercised the macOS Hub after the sidebar-color fix and uncovered issues in saved server identity, reachability, attention state, and search behavior. The round-three and round-four review passes found persistence edge cases that the first fix had not covered. Startup health now remains volatile for the entire session and cannot leak into the registry through later saves. Editing a server clears its startup overlay; palette cancellation clears stale results; health changes update Dock badge aggregation; and web-page errors only trigger health checks when they indicate connectivity failure.

The native Hub test suite passed (187 passed, 7 skipped). The final `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed remotely and locally, including all changed-path test files, rendered contrast, and UI smoke. A single unrelated timing-sensitive RepoOS test failed on the first remote attempt, passed in isolation locally, and passed in the final full check.

Earlier QA runs unintentionally wrote health fields into Nick's normal saved registry. That violated the task's isolation requirement. This round did not access or modify that external file; this worktree has no pre-QA copy to restore safely. The implementation and tests now prevent startup checks from contaminating a later save.

## Work and rationale

The QA isolation control is `REPOOS_HUB_SUPPORT_DIRECTORY`, documented in `macos/README.md`. Startup health refresh now stores status, check time, and health-derived identity in a volatile map separate from `ServerRegistryDocument`. UI entries are composed from persisted data plus that map. Route visits, selection, preference changes, pinning, and ordering save the document without persisting the overlay. Reordering explicitly restores persisted health and identity fields before writing. An explicit health refresh can still persist its result. Editing a server removes that server's volatile overlay before publishing the saved name and Healthy state.

Regression coverage exercises both persistence stages: the startup test performs a route visit after an Offline sweep and verifies that the saved status, timestamp, and edit time remain unchanged; the editor test then checks that a successful rename after an Offline startup sweep removes the overlay and persists Healthy state. The round-four bug was possible because the first volatile implementation overlaid name and health after any editor save, so the edited name could appear old and the row could remain Offline despite a successful verification.

Cross-server task search retains the current valid query while health updates cancel obsolete work and rerun against updated entries. User cancellation clears the query, remote results, and per-server status lines so a reopened Cmd-K palette cannot show previous-query results with an empty field. Tests cover both health-change reruns and completed-search cancellation.

WebKit failures expose a connectivity classification: Offline, TLS, and timeout trigger server health refresh; HTTP status, blocked navigation, and unknown errors do not. Retry still reloads the page. Sidebar and tab attention counts and their details popover are hidden while a server is not Healthy. `HubAppState` also sends volatile health changes to the attention coordinator without restarting its scheduler. Dock badge aggregation counts only Healthy servers, so stale totals from offline servers do not contribute.

Earlier review fixes remain: sidebar subtitles show saved origins; the auth-less serve banner matches its loopback-only bind; and the isolated registry environment variable is documented. No signing identity or app binary was added, and `repoos.toml` was not edited.

## Approaches tried

A `persistToDisk: false` argument around the immediate store write did not isolate startup health because it still mutated the document. Ordinary navigation subsequently called `persistQuietly`, flushing the change. Moving status to an overlay outside the document fixes that entire class of later-save behavior instead of requiring every save path to strip health fields.

For editor saves, the failing overlay was removed at the explicit successful-edit transition. The test uses a sequential checker to first produce Offline startup state and then a successful editor verification. For search, preserving the query across internal reconfiguration while keeping `cancel()` destructive gives different, testable semantics for health refresh versus dismissing the palette. For Dock badges, the coordinator receives fresh entries when health changes, and the aggregation policy independently rejects unhealthy entries.

## Challenges and blockers

The principal engineering difficulty was keeping presentation state and persisted state distinct across many paths that save the same document. A test that ends immediately after the sweep was insufficient; the test now performs a later unrelated write. The other challenge was that health flows to several consumers beyond the sidebar, including cross-server search, local-service context actions, attention counts, and the Dock badge.

QA screenshots are stored and attached in the task drawer: `.repoos/qa-screenshots/01-empty-dark.png`, `02-repoos-control-loaded.png`, `03-offline-row-before-relaunch.png`, and `04-offline-after-relaunch.png`. They were captured with `screencapture -l<windowid>` and visually inspected. They show the initial dark shell, loaded RepoOS page, and offline state before and after relaunch. Earlier round-one captures for light mode, add/edit/remove, Settings, and Cmd-K were referenced previously but were not available inside this worktree during later rounds, so they were not attached or re-inspected. This round did not launch the Hub again; code changes were checked with native tests.

The first round-four native run found test-fixture mistakes: one Dock test had default-Unknown entries despite expecting their badge totals, and the editor checker returned Offline for both startup and save. The fixtures were corrected; the rerun passed with 187 tests and 7 skips. The first final scoped RepoOS check had one unrelated `agent-review.test.ts` assertion fail (`expected 409, received 400`) under remote full-suite load. Its targeted case passed locally, and the second full scoped check passed with 123 test files (2,136 passed, 1 skipped), two additional boot timing tests, rendered contrast, and UI smoke.

## Key learnings

A write-suppression flag does not make shared mutable state volatile. Keep health data outside the persisted document from the start of a startup sweep, and test it after a normal subsequent save. Any reachability transition must update every dependent presentation surface, not just the status icon. Cancellation also needs an explicit contract: clearing background work without clearing its visible results leaves stale UI behind even after a panel is dismissed.

The earlier QA launches changed health fields in the normal registry. Review documented those writes, and I did not touch the external registry in this round. Without a pre-QA copy, the original values cannot be reconstructed from the worktree; restoring them by guessing would risk additional corruption.
